| `DataType` C weight standardisation — potentially a third of the archive, against 0.08% for the weight repeats that remain | untested |
| Whether excluding `SpeciesSex` from the weight key loses anything | untested |
| The intersection of the duplicated length series with the records whose weight is still summed twice — predicted empty | not computed |


# Appendices

Reference and evidence material, moved out of the reading path. Nothing
here is required to follow the argument; all of it is cited from the text
where it matters.


The weight questions that remain share one instrument that has not been built:
**mean weight per fish, `w_haul / n_haul`, stratified by species**. That
quantity is biologically bounded within roughly an order of magnitude, so any
mechanism that scales weight without scaling number leaves a self-normalising
signature — which is what makes the whole family testable at once. The
individual cases, with their tests, are in `PLAN-qc-checks.md` section 8.

## Building CPUEL from `HL_length` {#building-cpuel-from-hl_length}

The clearest way to see that these are the same table is to build one from the
other. CPUEL's payload is numbers per hour by haul, species and length class —
`.id`, `aphia`, `length_mm`, `n_hour` — with `sex` empty throughout.
`HL_length` is finer than that in three ways it keeps on purpose (sex,
development stage and length measurement type), so CPUEL is one aggregation
away:

```{r}
cpuel_like <- dr_con("HL_length") |>
  filter(Survey == "NS-IBTS", Year == 2023, Quarter == 1) |>
  group_by(.id, Valid_Aphia, length_mm) |>
  summarise(n_hour = sum(n_hour, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
```

Set that against ICES's own file for the same hauls:

```{r}
cpuel <- duckdbfs::open_dataset("https://heima.hafro.is/~einarhj/datras/CPUEL.parquet") |>
  filter(Survey == "NS-IBTS", Year == 2023, Quarter == 1, n_hour > 0) |>
  select(.id, Valid_Aphia = aphia, length_mm, cpuel = n_hour)

cpuel_like |>
  inner_join(cpuel, by = c(".id", "Valid_Aphia", "length_mm")) |>
  summarise(cells = n(),
            agree = sum(ifelse(abs(n_hour - cpuel) < 0.001, 1, 0))) |>
  collect()
```

Over the 317 hauls both sides cover, the rebuild matches **96.6% of CPUEL's
non-zero cells** and agrees with **96.45%** of those to a thousandth of a fish
per hour. A worked haul, three cod:

```{r}
cpuel_like |>
  inner_join(cpuel, by = c(".id", "Valid_Aphia", "length_mm")) |>
  filter(.id == "NS-IBTS:2023:1:DE:06NI:GOV:104:22", Valid_Aphia == 126436) |>
  arrange(length_mm) |>
  collect()
```

The causes of the residual are named, though not quantified: nothing in it has
been traced to the arithmetic. The two files are independent downloads with
their own calculation vintages, so a haul revised on one side and not the
other differs, and this comparison cannot tell that apart from a genuine
disagreement. On BITS two further, documented things apply: CPUEL gear-standardises cod and nothing else and does not
always preserve the submitted length grid — both of which a
generalised product would have to decide about explicitly rather than inherit.

**The zero rows are the part that is not one aggregation away**, and
deliberately so. Half of CPUEL is explicit zeros — 5,874,543 of 11,774,468
rows, each carrying `length_mm = 0` — and they encode a judgement about which
species were in scope for a haul. Add them yourself and the judgement stays
yours:

```{r}
hauls   <- cpuel_like |> distinct(.id) |> collect()
species <- cpuel_like |> distinct(Valid_Aphia) |> collect()    # your universe, not ours

tidyr::crossing(hauls, species) |>
  left_join(collect(cpuel_like), by = c(".id", "Valid_Aphia")) |>
  tidyr::replace_na(list(n_hour = 0, length_mm = 0))
```

On this one survey-quarter that turns 318 hauls and 141 species into 81,557
rows, 38,513 of them explicit zeros — the same roughly-half proportion CPUEL
carries, arrived at from a universe you chose rather than one you inherited.

That is the whole distance between `HL_length` and a CPUEL product covering
29 surveys rather than 8: one `group_by()`, plus a species universe that only a
survey group can properly set.

## Existing analyses run on them unchanged

A product also has to leave standing what is already built on the exchange
tables. So: starting from these two tables instead of the raw HL record, can
the usual chain still be run — numbers at length raised to the haul, summed to
total numbers and weight per haul, divided by swept area and carried through to
a stratified abundance index?

`data-raw/CHECK_datras_adapter.R` answers that against real numbers. It
assembles an object whose HL comes **only** from `HL_length` and `HL_summary`,
never from raw HL, runs [`{DATRAS}`](https://github.com/DTUAqua/DATRAS) and
`{DATRASextra}` on it unmodified, and compares with the same steps run on their
own bundled fixture — NS-IBTS 2020–2023, quarters 1 and 3, dab (*Limanda
limanda*), 2,651 valid hauls. The adapter is about 60 lines: rename to the
legacy field names, add the five HH quantities the packages derive for
themselves, and reshape the two catch tables into the single HL frame they
expect. **No arithmetic on any number** — the raised number at length is
`n_haul` exactly as published.

| Step | Quantity | Difference |
|---|---|---|
| numbers at length, by length class | `N`, 41 classes | same classes, **max gap 0** over 108,691 cells |
| total numbers per haul | `HaulN` | **max gap 0** over 2,651 hauls |
| total weight per haul, from the length–weight lookup | `HaulWgt` | **max gap 0** |
| swept area | `SweptArea` | **max gap 0** |
| stratified abundance index, per hour, by statistical rectangle | index and CV | **identical** |

Eleven checks, no differences (re-run 2026-09-08). The last of them is the
figure a survey working group would report, and it comes out the same to every
digit:

```
  Year    index         cv
  2020 771.7314 0.07114170
  2021 712.8609 0.09926699
  2022 823.4249 0.06559173
  2023 739.3506 0.05788805
```

Two caveats. Species recorded in a haul but never measured enter through
`HL_summary`, carrying no length — which is how the exchange format carries
them, and what a species-richness count needs; a length table alone would lose
them. And **CA is out of scope**: `{obus}` derives no age table, so nothing
age-, maturity- or individual-weight-based is exercised.

Underneath sits the field-by-field comparison,
`data-raw/CHECK_datras_interop.R` — 25 checks, no differences, including the
raised number at length (max gap 2.3 × 10⁻¹³ over 24,960 cells) and the
measured number at length, `NumberAtLength`, against `n_measured` (max gap 0 over
16,196 cells).


## Field names: two layers, both ICES's {#two-naming-layers}

Field names in this codebase come from two places — **both of them ICES's** —
and there is deliberately no third.

| Layer | What it is | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **1. ICES legacy exchange names** | The names the exchange file still carries, and the ones the older ICES documents quoted here use. | `HLNoAtLngt`, `SubFactor`, `CatIdentifier` |
| **2. ICES current names** | ICES's replacement names, published in the current field descriptions. What the raw parquet archive carries, and what every `{obus}` table carries too. | `NumberAtLength`, `SubsamplingFactor`, `SpeciesCategory` |

**The translation between the two layers is ICES's own, not this package's.**
ICES is renaming DATRAS's fields table by table, and publishes the
old-to-new pairs itself in two places: the `getDatrasFieldList` operation on
the DATRAS web service, which returns each current `FieldName` alongside the
`FieldNameOld` it was renamed from, and the *DATRAS New Headers Lookup*
spreadsheet of December 2024 [@ices2024newheaders], which carries the same
pairs in one sheet per record type. Layer 2 is therefore not a scheme `{opus}`
invented and `{obus}` adopted — it is ICES's own target naming, taken up ahead of
the migration's completion. The migration's progress is visible in the service:
HL has flipped, and `getHLdataNewHeaders` returns all 29 of its fields under
the current names, while HH, CA and LT are still served under legacy names
only.

The documentation has already moved ahead of the service: the current field
descriptions name every field in layer 2, so a reader working from ICES's
workbook and a reader working from the `{obus}` tables see the same column names.
Legacy names survive in four places:

- the exchange files themselves;
- the web-service operations that have not yet flipped;
- the older ICES documents quoted later in this article;
- and, in a handful of cells, the current descriptions' own prose — where
  formulas still read `TotalNo=SUM(HLNoAtLngt)` and *"If DataType is C,
  CatIdentifier is always 1"* beneath fields now called `TotalNumber` and
  `SpeciesCategory`.

Quotations below keep whatever names the quoted document uses.

**`{obus}` invents no field names.** `dr_con_raw("HL")` and `dr_con("HL_length")`
both carry `Valid_Aphia` and `SpeciesSex`, so a join between the raw archive and
a derived table needs no name mapping, and the crosswalk below describes every
column in every table.

A shorter `sex` column is a tempting simplification, and it is the wrong one.
ICES's legacy `Sex` maps to `SpeciesSex` in HL but to `IndividualSex` in CA —
two genuinely different measurements, one a property of a length-frequency
record and the other of an individual fish. A single `sex` column flattens
them.

### The legacy-to-current crosswalk

The mapping is neither hand-authored here nor taken from ICES's published
lists on trust. `{opus}` checks every pair ICES publishes against the field names
the corresponding operation actually returns, keeps what survives
(`opus::op_datras_field_list()`), reduces that to a collision-checked 1:1 map
(`opus::op_datras_rename_crosswalk()`), and embeds the result in the raw
parquet footer. `{obus}` reads it back from the same file as the data, so it
cannot describe a different vintage than the data it accompanies:

```{r}
opus::op_crosswalk("HL")
```

29 rows — two more than either ICES list. Neither `getDatrasFieldList` nor the
December 2024 lookup documents HL's `DateofCalculation` or `Valid_Aphia` under
any name, though both are real fields that `getHLdata` and
`getHLdataNewHeaders` alike return; they appear here unrenamed, which is what
those two operations show them to be.

Check names against this output rather than from memory. Most pairs
are guessable; at least one is not — **`LenMeasType` maps to `LengthType`**,
which is easy to mistake for a length *unit* field when it is a measurement
*convention* field. `Sex` → `SpeciesSex` is the pair worth memorising, because ICES's one legacy
`Sex` splits across two current names — `SpeciesSex` in HL and
`IndividualSex` in CA — so it is the clearest case of why the crosswalk is
per table rather than global.


## An engineering note: R and SQL disagree about `NA`

Not a DATRAS matter, but the single largest source of silent defects in this
code. `{obus}` runs the same functions eagerly (data frames, in the tests) and
lazily (DuckDB, in the build), and the two backends differ in four ways.
Anyone extending these functions needs all four.

**1. Joining.** SQL treats `NULL = NULL` as unknown, so a lazy join drops
every row with an `NA` key — and `SpeciesSex` is `NA` in 54% of HL, with
`SpeciesCategory`, `SpeciesValidity` and `TotalNumber` able to be `NA` too.
Every join in `dr_HL_summary()` whose key can hold `NA` carries
`na_matches = "na"`, which dbplyr renders as `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` and DuckDB
supports natively. Without it, every `NA`-sex row fails to find its own
length-derived expectation, never reconciles, falls to the fallback, and
undercounts. Confirmed on a real case
(`BITS:1999:1:DK:26HI:TVS:017492:22`, aphia 127143): true total 4, and 3
without the flag.

**2. Aggregating over an all-`NA` group.** `sum(x, na.rm = TRUE)` is `0` in R
and `NULL` in SQL. Every aggregation here carries an explicit non-`NA` counter
(`.n_ok`, `.h_ok`, `.w_ok`, `.wh_ok`) and forces `NA` when the counter is
zero, so both backends agree. Without it the eager path silently converts a
deliberate `NA` — a missing `SubsamplingFactor`, a non-positive
`HaulDuration`, a species that was never weighed — straight back into the
confident `0` it was meant to prevent.

**3. Self-reference inside `summarise()`.** dplyr evaluates expressions in
order, so `n_ok = sum(!is.na(n_haul))` written *after* `n_haul = sum(n_haul)`
sees the new scalar; SQL resolves every aggregate against the source column.
`dr_HL_length()` renames to `.n_raw`/`.h_raw` before aggregating, so the two
agree by construction rather than by luck.

**4. String concatenation with `NA`.** On a plain data frame R's `paste(sep =)`
renders an `NA` field as the literal two-character string `"NA"`; on a
`tbl_lazy`, dbplyr translates the same call to DuckDB's `CONCAT_WS()`, which
drops `NA` fields instead. `.id` is the join key between HH, HL and CA, so it
must come out identical whichever backend built it. `.dr_concat_ws()` builds
the `NA`-skipping behaviour explicitly from `is.na()`, `case_when()` and
`paste0()`, which translate the same way on both — with one deliberate
departure from raw `CONCAT_WS()`: when every field is `NA` it returns `NA`,
not `CONCAT_WS()`'s `""`, because an empty string would collide every such row
onto one `.id`.

Each of these produced a real, silent, wrong number at some point. Keeping
both an eager test suite and a lazy build is what catches them; neither does
alone.


## Why the two routes disagree

[Part III](#two-routes-to-a-catch-total) shows that the submitted `TotalNumber`
and the raised length rows differ by a fish or more in 133,874 groups. Most of
that has one mechanism, and it is arithmetic done before the file was
submitted.

Define `F = TotalNumber / SubsampledNumber` — the whole multiplier the
submitter actually used, read straight off the record with nothing
reconstructed. Split `DataType` `C` groups by whether that multiplier is a
whole number:

```{r}
dr_con("HL") |>
  inner_join(dr_con("HH") |> select(.id, DataType), by = ".id") |>
  filter(DataType == "C", Survey != "Can-Mar", !is.na(LengthClass),
         NumberAtLength != 0, !is.na(TotalNumber),
         !is.na(SubsampledNumber), SubsampledNumber > 0) |>
  group_by(.id, Valid_Aphia, SpeciesCategory, SpeciesValidity, SpeciesSex) |>
  summarise(s   = sum(NumberAtLength, na.rm = TRUE),
            tot = max(TotalNumber, na.rm = TRUE),
            sub = max(SubsampledNumber, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(whole_number_factor = abs(tot / sub - round(tot / sub)) < 1e-9) |>
  group_by(whole_number_factor) |>
  summarise(groups = n(),
            whole_fish_gap = sum(as.integer(abs(tot - s) >= 1)), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(rate_pct = round(100 * whole_fish_gap / groups, 2)) |>
  collect()
```

0.19% against 29.49% — a relative risk of about 150, using no reconstruction
whatsoever. A non-integer multiplier is the single strongest predictor of a
whole-fish disagreement in the archive.

The mechanism follows. If the submitter raised each length row separately,
`round(NumberAtLength / F)` should recover the raw integer counts, and those
should sum to the `SubsampledNumber` the record reports independently:

```{r}
dr_con("HL") |>
  inner_join(dr_con("HH") |> select(.id, DataType), by = ".id") |>
  filter(DataType == "C", Survey != "Can-Mar", !is.na(LengthClass),
         NumberAtLength != 0, !is.na(TotalNumber),
         !is.na(SubsampledNumber), SubsampledNumber > 0) |>
  mutate(F = TotalNumber / SubsampledNumber) |>
  filter(F > 0) |>
  mutate(m = round(NumberAtLength / F)) |>
  group_by(.id, Valid_Aphia, SpeciesCategory, SpeciesValidity, SpeciesSex) |>
  summarise(F = max(F, na.rm = TRUE), sum_m = sum(m, na.rm = TRUE),
            sub = max(SubsampledNumber, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(whole_number_factor = abs(F - round(F)) < 1e-9) |>
  summarise(groups = n(),
            reconstruction_matches = sum(as.integer(abs(sum_m - sub) < 0.5)),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  collect()
```

It does, in 86% of the non-integer groups. So the submitter computed
`NumberAtLength = round(m * F)` row by row while computing `TotalNumber` once
over the whole sample. The per-row rounding residuals do not cancel, and their
sum is the gap. **The fish are missing from the submitted file before `{obus}`
reads it**, which is why no choice in the derivation can recover them.

## Can-Mar

Can-Mar behaves differently enough to be worth separating. The article used to
record two candidate mechanisms and no way to choose between them: a raising
factor lost in a provider-side conversion, or fish counted into `TotalNumber`
that never entered a length row. They make different predictions, so they can
be told apart.

**A lost conversion would apply to a whole haul.** If a factor went missing in
processing, every species in that haul should show the same ratio of reported
total to measured lengths. Take Can-Mar hauls where three or more species show
a gap at `SubsamplingFactor` 1, and ask how many carry one shared ratio:

```{r}
dr_con("HL") |>
  inner_join(dr_con("HH") |> select(.id, DataType), by = ".id") |>
  filter(Survey == "Can-Mar", DataType %in% c("R", "P", "S"),
         !is.na(LengthClass), NumberAtLength != 0) |>
  group_by(.id, Valid_Aphia) |>
  summarise(s = sum(NumberAtLength, na.rm = TRUE),
            f = max(SubsamplingFactor, na.rm = TRUE),
            tot = max(TotalNumber, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(!is.na(tot), !is.na(f), f == 1, s > 0, tot - s >= 1) |>
  group_by(.id) |>
  summarise(species = n(), distinct_ratios = n_distinct(round(tot / s, 3)),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(species >= 3) |>
  summarise(hauls                 = n(),
            all_species_one_ratio = sum(as.integer(distinct_ratios == 1)),
            any_two_agree         = sum(as.integer(distinct_ratios < species)),
            every_ratio_different = sum(as.integer(distinct_ratios == species))) |>
  collect()
```

Not one haul in 4,523 has a single ratio across its species. In 4,225 of them
every species has a different one, and in only 298 do even two species agree.
**The lost-factor reading is refuted**, at least as anything applied at haul
level.

**The other mechanism predicts whole fish.** Fish counted but never measured
leave an integer gap, and they leave the record's own sub-sample field siding
with the length rows rather than with the total:

```{r}
dr_con("HL") |>
  inner_join(dr_con("HH") |> select(.id, DataType), by = ".id") |>
  filter(Survey == "Can-Mar", DataType %in% c("R", "P", "S"),
         !is.na(LengthClass), NumberAtLength != 0) |>
  group_by(.id, Valid_Aphia) |>
  summarise(s = sum(NumberAtLength, na.rm = TRUE),
            f = max(SubsamplingFactor, na.rm = TRUE),
            sub = max(SubsampledNumber, na.rm = TRUE),
            tot = max(TotalNumber, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(!is.na(tot), !is.na(f), f == 1, s > 0, tot - s >= 1) |>
  summarise(groups         = n(),
            gap_whole_fish = sum(as.integer(abs((tot - s) - round(tot - s)) < 1e-9)),
            sub_eq_lengths = sum(as.integer(abs(sub - s) < 0.5)),
            sub_eq_total   = sum(as.integer(abs(sub - tot) < 0.5)),
            gap_of_1       = sum(as.integer(tot - s == 1)),
            gap_over_10    = sum(as.integer(tot - s > 10))) |>
  collect()
```

Every one of the 25,953 gaps is a whole number of fish — unlike the rounding
mechanism above, which leaves fractional residues. Where `SubsampledNumber` is
present it matches the length rows in 10,183 groups and the total in **none**.
So the record's own account of what was measured corroborates the lengths, and
`TotalNumber` alone carries the extra fish: exactly one fish in 4,239 groups,
more than ten in 12,647.

**What is left open.** This refutes a haul-level conversion and fits fish
counted but not measured. It does not exclude a factor lost per species, though
the ratios tell against that too: they concentrate on 4/3, 3/2, 5/4, 6/5 and
7/6, which are what a handful of unmeasured fish produce and implausible as
sub-sampling factors — nobody sub-samples a catch at eight sevenths. Treat
Can-Mar separately and prefer the reported total.

**For ICES.** Does Can-Mar record fish in `TotalNumber` that are deliberately
not length-measured, and if so, is that intended under the format?

## Duplicated length series {#duplicated-length-series}

This is the one place where `{obus}`'s choice of what makes a row unique
measurably moves the number. One BITS record, one species, and the whole length
series written twice under two `LengthType` codes:

```{r}
dr_con("HL") |>
  filter(.id == "BITS:2017:4:DK:26HF:TVS:552:42", Valid_Aphia == 127082) |>
  group_by(LengthType) |>
  summarise(length_rows       = n(),
            sum_NumberAtLength = sum(NumberAtLength, na.rm = TRUE),
            SubsampledNumber  = max(SubsampledNumber, na.rm = TRUE),
            TotalNumber       = max(TotalNumber, na.rm = TRUE),
            SpeciesCategoryWeight = max(SpeciesCategoryWeight, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  collect()
```

Two identical series. Every one of the 19 length classes appears under both
codes carrying the same count, and both copies report the same
`SubsampledNumber` 57, the same `TotalNumber` 57 and the same 4500 g.
`dr_HL_length()` treats `LengthType` as part of what makes a row unique, so it
adds both copies and returns 114 where `TotalNumber` reports 57 — a ratio of
exactly 2.

How far this reaches:

```{r}
dr_con("HL_length") |>
  group_by(.id, Valid_Aphia, SpeciesValidity, SpeciesSex, DevelopmentStage,
           length_mm, accuracy) |>
  summarise(length_types = n_distinct(LengthType),
            distinct_counts = n_distinct(n_measured), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(length_types > 1, distinct_counts == 1) |>
  summarise(duplicated_rows = n(),
            haul_species_groups = n_distinct(paste0(.id, "|", Valid_Aphia))) |>
  collect()
```

**These look like coding artefacts rather than two real measurement
conventions.** `LengthType` codes are supposed to be different length
definitions, so the same fish measured both ways would give *different*
`LengthClass` values. Series identical in length class, count, sub-sample,
total and weight cannot be two genuine measurements of one catch. *What would
settle it:* confirming with ICES that the codes are non-convertible
measurement definitions.

`{obus}` does not merge them, because `LengthType` genuinely splits other
records, and merging on a hypothesis would lose those.

## The same weight written on two category codes

Keeping the category is right when two categories are two separately weighed
parts of the catch. It is wrong when the same weight has simply been written on
two codes — and under **pseudo-category sampling (`DataType` P) that is the
documented convention**, not an error. The pseudo-category memo states
*"CatCatchweight value is same in each subcategory"*, and the archive agrees:

```{r}
dr_con("HL") |>
  inner_join(dr_con("HH") |> select(.id, DataType), by = ".id") |>
  filter(DataType == "P", !is.na(SpeciesCategory)) |>
  mutate(main_category = substr(SpeciesCategory, 1, 1)) |>
  distinct(.id, Valid_Aphia, SpeciesValidity, main_category,
           SpeciesCategory, SpeciesCategoryWeight) |>
  group_by(.id, Valid_Aphia, SpeciesValidity, main_category) |>
  summarise(sub_categories = n_distinct(SpeciesCategory),
            distinct_weights = n_distinct(SpeciesCategoryWeight), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(sub_categories > 1) |>
  summarise(main_categories = n(),
            one_shared_weight = sum(as.integer(distinct_weights == 1))) |>
  collect()
```

1,456 of 1,464 — 99.5% carry a single identical weight across their
sub-categories, which is the convention the memo describes. The structural reason is in the sampling
itself — under P the raising factor *is* category weight divided by sample
weight, so the category weight must appear on every sub-category row of that
category.

**`{obus}` therefore collapses P weights on the main category**, not on the
reported code. Under P the `SpeciesCategory` is two digits, the first being the
main category, so `11`, `12` and `13` are one weighing and not three. Take the
worked case that used to be wrong:

```{r}
dr_con_raw("HL") |>
  dr_add_id() |>
  filter(.id == "NS-IBTS:2016:1:GB-SCT:748S:GOV:12:12", Valid_Aphia == 126437) |>
  distinct(SpeciesCategory, TotalNumber, SpeciesCategoryWeight) |>
  collect()
```

Both sub-categories carry 105,300 g, which is one catch weighed once.
`HL_summary` returns it once:

```{r}
dr_con("HL_summary") |>
  filter(.id == "NS-IBTS:2016:1:GB-SCT:748S:GOV:12:12", Valid_Aphia == 126437) |>
  select(n_totalnumber, w_haul) |> collect()
```

Left uncollapsed this one haul would report 210,600 g for a 105,300 g catch,
and archive-wide the P repeats were worth 410,122,351 g — close to 29% of all
`DataType` P weight mass, because sub-category sampling is used precisely on
the big catches. The records are still marked, as `WGT_CAT_REPEAT_P` in
`dr_con("hl_flag")`, with `kind` `property`: the flag records that the
submission carries the repetition, not that the published weight is wrong.

**What is deliberately not collapsed.** The same shape occurs under `DataType`
R, where ICES documents no sub-category convention at all, and there the cause
is not established: of 209 such records, 135 are a single platform and year
(NS-IBTS 2025 Q3, GB, platform 74E9), and among those where `TotalNumber` also
differs some ties look implausible (two categories both at exactly 9,992 g) and
some entirely plausible (two tiny catches both at 12 g). Collapsing them would
assert a convention no document states, so `{obus}` sums them and flags them
`WGT_CAT_REPEAT_R`, `kind` `unexplained`. A further 36 P records share one
weight *across* main categories, which the memo does not describe either.

Together those are the whole of the remaining excess. Set the published
`w_haul` against the alternative of collapsing every repeated weight whatever
the `DataType`:

```{r}
published <- dr_con("HL_summary") |>
  group_by(.id, Valid_Aphia, SpeciesValidity) |>
  summarise(w_pub = sum(w_haul, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

collapsed <- dr_con_raw("HL") |>
  dr_add_id() |>
  inner_join(dr_con_raw("HH") |> dr_add_id() |> select(.id, DataType), by = ".id") |>
  filter(DataType != "C") |>
  distinct(.id, Valid_Aphia, SpeciesValidity, SpeciesCategoryWeight, DataType) |>
  group_by(.id, Valid_Aphia, SpeciesValidity, DataType) |>
  summarise(w_alt = sum(SpeciesCategoryWeight, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

published |>
  inner_join(collapsed, by = c(".id", "Valid_Aphia", "SpeciesValidity")) |>
  filter(w_pub > w_alt + 0.5) |>
  group_by(DataType) |>
  summarise(records = n(), excess_g = sum(w_pub - w_alt)) |>
  collect()
```

**18,513,763 g in all — 0.080% of the archive's `w_haul` mass** of
23,263,243,838 g. Before the P collapse the same comparison returned
428,460,512 g, or 1.84%. The flag table marks 1,491 P and 209 R records.

**The numbers are unaffected either way.** For all 1,491 P repeated-weight
records the underlying length frequencies **differ**, so the mechanism that
repeats a weight never touches `n_haul`. Conversely the weight path ignores
`DevelopmentStage` and `LengthType`, so the [duplicated length
series](#duplicated-length-series) that inflate `n_haul` cannot
inflate `w_haul` there. The two affected sets are expected to be disjoint; that
has **not been computed**, and a non-empty result would be a new finding.


## How this article was made {#how-this-article-was-made}

**What counts as evidence.** Every claim is either a quotation from an ICES
document or a measurement of the archive, and the measurements are given as
code that reads the published tables directly, so they need nothing but the
package.

**A note on the numbers, because DATRAS grows.** The structural counts — how
many rows each table has, how many haul x species groups, how many of those
carry no length data — are **measured when this article is rendered**, not
typed in, so they cannot drift apart from each other or from the archive. The
analytical figures are different: the CPUEL reconciliation, the rounding
regimes, the confidence intervals took real work to establish, and re-running
them on every render would embed whole analyses in a reference article. Those
are stated once, as dated evidence, and the claims they support are written in
the form that survives the archive growing — *only*, *exactly one*, *never* —
so that if one ever stops being true, that is a finding rather than a stale
number.

**On the package.** [`{obus}`](https://github.com/einarhjorleifsson/obus) is a
reference implementation of the proposal and a demonstration that it holds for
the whole archive rather than part of it. Every rule it applies is quoted from
an ICES document; every figure is reproducible from the published archive with
the code shown. The nearest thing to a proof of the proposal is that [CPUEL
itself can be rebuilt from `HL_length`](#building-cpuel-from-hl_length),
worked through above.
